title: But how does bitcoin actually work?
beats: What does it mean to have a Bitcoin? Promise: walk through how you would have invented it
Path: ledger among friends, less trust, add cryptography; also says details not needed to use it
Communal ledger among friends (Alice, Bob, Charlie), settle monthly
Problem: anyone can add a line; Bob writes Alice pays Bob $100
Digital signatures via PK/SK; sign and verify as two functions, 2^256 scale
Loophole: replaying a signed line; fix with unique ID
Honor-system settling fails (Charlie); pre-fund and reject overspending
Ledger dollars; first key point: the ledger is the currency
Everyone keeps own copy; how can all agree on order? Posed as a puzzle to the viewer
Answer teased: trust the ledger with most computational work
Cryptographic hash function: fixed-size, looks random, tiny change flips output
No proof hashes are hard to invert, yet security depends on it
Special number making 30 leading zeros: about a billion guesses, instant check
Blocks, prev-hash links, rewrite cascades through chain
Miners listen, build blocks, get reward; mining as miniature lottery
Attack walk-through: Alice forges a fork; needs near 50 percent compute; wait several blocks
Real-world details: 10 minute difficulty, halving, 21M cap, fees, throughput vs Visa

theory: The video makes the viewer the inventor: every mechanism is introduced as a patch for a failure that was just shown, so no component appears before its need. Trust is rebuilt layer by layer until the only remaining question has been posed aloud, so the answer lands as relief.
velocity: Orchestrator: sequence a playbook as a failure chain, with each new tool gated on a visible break in the previous model
Scene builder: a 'cheater' ghost-actor that tries attacks on the current protocol state
Voice: pose the unsolved puzzle explicitly and pause before revealing the answer
Learner model: record which failure each concept patched, and quiz by asking what breaks without it
Evals: check toy parameters appear before real ones, and real ones are revealed later
quote: no cold hard rigorous proof that it's hard to compute in reverse
